enrichment.short_title: ASBO application against street prostitute — meaning of 'likely' and aggregation of conduct

statutes_considered.title: Police Reform Act 2002
provisions: amendments to section 1 Crime and Disorder Act 1998

key_facts: The Chief Constable of Lancashire appealed by case stated after Preston magistrates refused an anti-social behaviour order against Lisa Marie Potter, a street prostitute operating in residential areas of Preston between February and April 2002.

Police evidence showed prostitution caused substantial quality-of-life problems including kerb crawling, drug-related activity and occasional aggravated conduct by other prostitutes; Potter's own conduct was limited to loitering and soliciting.

The deputy district judge applied the criminal standard of proof to all constituents of section 1(1)(a), refused to aggregate Potter's conduct with that of other prostitutes, and found actual or likely harassment, alarm or distress not proved.
The judge indicated that on the balance of probabilities he would have found likelihood satisfied, but treated 'not necessarily' as 'no' when applying the criminal standard.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Preston Magistrates' Court to the Divisional Court (Administrative Court).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to the deputy district judge to reconsider section 1(1)(a) (including aggregation) and, if satisfied, necessity and discretion under section 1(1)(b) and section 1(4).
enrichment.ratio: On an ASBO application under section 1(1)(a), 'likely' to cause harassment, alarm or distress means more probable than not, and that likelihood must be proved to the criminal standard; courts must not conflate proof of actual causation with proof of likelihood, and may consider a defendant's conduct together with that of others when assessing effect even without proof of concerted or aggravated behaviour.
legal_issues: Whether 'likely' in section 1(1)(a) requires proof to the criminal standard and what threshold 'likely' denotes
Whether a defendant's anti-social conduct may be aggregated with that of others not acting in concert
Whether the magistrates' refusal of the ASBO was perverse on the evidence

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor's appeal against fines for costs failures, absent taxation hearing and abusive letters
key_facts: Michael John Darby, sole practitioner in Halesowen, was found guilty by the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal of five allegations of conduct unbefitting arising from his retainer for client Mr L in litigation over a £460 building contract dispute with Mrs C in Caernarfon.

Darby failed for years to comply with Rule 15 on costs information, refused at short notice to attend a taxation hearing unless Mr L paid £2,000 on account despite never having rendered a bill, and wrote offensive letters to Mr L, his wife, his mother, Mrs G and his bank manager pressing for payment.
The litigation left Mr L facing over £50,000 in costs on a small original claim; the Tribunal fined Darby £3,000 on each of five offences and ordered costs assessed at £19,586.30.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 49 of the Solicitors Act 1974 to the Administrative Court by way of rehearing against Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal findings and penalty.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed in its entirety; fines of £15,000 total and costs order upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to provide timely Rule 15 costs information to a client embarking on high-risk legally aided litigation, refusing to attend a taxation hearing for want of unbilled payments, and writing offensive confidential letters to third parties each amount to serious conduct unbefitting a solicitor; the Tribunal's penalty assessment warrants strong deference absent clear disproportionality.
legal_issues: Whether Darby breached Rule 15 and whether any breach was sufficiently serious to constitute misconduct
Whether refusing to attend the taxation hearing without reasonable notice was a breach of duty to client and court
Whether separate penalties for overlapping letter-writing offences were permissible
Whether overall fines and costs were disproportionate

enrichment.short_title: Homeless British mother denied priority need because dependant child subject to immigration control
key_facts: The claimant, a British citizen by descent from Mauritius, cares for her two-year-old Mauritian daughter who remains subject to immigration control.

After becoming homeless in Westminster, she was eligible for assistance but Westminster City Council refused priority need under section 189(1)(b), treating the child as disregarded under section 185(4).
The Council's section 192(3) discretion challenge was abandoned; the live dispute concerned construction of section 185(4) and alleged incompatibility with Convention rights.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of Westminster City Council's refusal to treat the claimant as in priority need; permission granted by Collins J after initial refusal.
enrichment.outcome: On ordinary construction, section 185(4) required the Council to disregard the daughter; further consideration of discrimination, section 3 reading and declaration of incompatibility adjourned pending formal Crown notice under CPR 19.4A.
enrichment.ratio: Section 185(2) identifies persons subject to immigration control as 'persons from abroad who are ineligible for housing assistance' within section 185(1), and section 185(4) requires such persons to be disregarded when determining whether another person has priority need under Part VII even where the parent is eligible.
legal_issues: Whether section 185(4) applies only to persons within section 185(1) as distinct from section 185(2)
Whether a child subject to immigration control but habitually resident may avoid being 'from abroad'
Whether Part VI allocation rules create inconsistency with Part VII priority need
Whether the construction violates Article 8 and Article 14 ECHR and whether section 3 or section 4 HRA relief is available

enrichment.short_title: Failure to provide breath specimen — delay in contacting duty solicitor before evidential procedure
key_facts: After a road traffic accident on 4 November 2002 the appellant was arrested at 5.30am, taken via hospital to Islington police station arriving at 7.25am, and at 7.40am requested a duty solicitor on the custody record.
Police Sergeant Barrett began the section 7 evidential breath procedure immediately while booking-in continued; the appellant refused specimens twice between 7.40 and 7.50am.
The duty solicitor call centre was contacted at 7.53am and the solicitor spoke to the appellant at 8.00am, after the procedure concluded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated against conviction at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court for failing to provide a breath specimen contrary to section 7(6) RTA 1988.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; district judge's conclusion that section 58 was complied with and Code C breach was insignificant was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Whether a custody officer acted without delay to secure legal advice and permitted consultation as soon as practicable is a question of fact and degree; in drink-drive investigations significant prior delay and immediate availability of the breath-test officer may justify proceeding before contacting the duty solicitor call centre, and minor Code C delay will not require exclusion under section 78 PACE.
legal_issues: Whether the custody officer breached section 58(4) PACE by not telephoning the duty solicitor before starting the breath procedure
Whether Code C paragraph 6.5 breach was significant and substantial
Whether breath-test evidence should be excluded under section 78 PACE

enrichment.short_title: Care proceedings — mother allowed to disclose papers to residential assessment unit
key_facts: SB, an 18-year-old mother, appealed the Redbridge Family Proceedings Court's refusal to permit disclosure of care proceedings papers to Jamma Umoja for a possible residential assessment.

Baby Bethany, born February 2002, had moved between grandmother, foster care and father before returning to foster care; threshold under section 31 was conceded and the local authority care plan was adoption.
Earlier referrals to Legard, Breslaff, Highlands and St Michael's Fellowships had failed or not been pursued; the mother sought a last chance to demonstrate capacity to parent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to High Court (Family Division) from Redbridge Family Proceedings Court directions hearing in ongoing care proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; permission granted to disclose papers to Jamma Umoja on terms that the fixed December 2003 outcome hearing must not be delayed.
enrichment.ratio: Justices may refuse disclosure of care papers to an assessment unit only where relevant factors support that exercise of discretion; here they took into account immaterial delay concerns and failed to weigh the finality of the adoption plan, the mother's youth, and her renewed motivation after the father's placement failed.
legal_issues: Whether justices erred in refusing leave to disclose court papers to Jamma Umoja
Whether further professional assessment would impermissibly delay final resolution for the child
Whether a provisional disclosure order precedes any section 38(6) residential assessment direction

enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal — tribunal not obliged to consider duplicate counsel application over appellant's own

statutes_considered.title: Immigration and Asylum Appeals Procedure Rules 2000

key_facts: Shahhosseini Hossein, an Iranian asylum seeker, had his appeal dismissed by an adjudicator who comprehensively rejected his credibility and authenticity of summons documents.

On 5 September 2002 both the appellant personally and his solicitors (via counsel's grounds faxed at 1.42pm) lodged leave applications; the IAT processed only the personal application and has no record of the fax.
The Vice President refused leave on the personal grounds; judicial review sought to compel consideration of counsel's application and alleged breach of legitimate expectation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of Immigration Appeal Tribunal refusal of leave to appeal against adjudicator's dismissal of asylum and human rights claims.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no obligation to consider more than one application and underlying claim lacked merit in any event.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 18 requires a single complete application for leave with all grounds; where an appellant lodges a valid personal application received before any later representative application, the Tribunal may proceed on that application without waiting or merging duplicate submissions, and no legitimate expectation arises that counsel's grounds will be considered if not received.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred by deciding leave on the appellant's personal application without considering counsel's faxed application
Whether acknowledgment to solicitors created a legitimate expectation
Whether the adjudicator's credibility findings and document authentication approach were flawed

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor's discipline appeal — delay, bias, conveyancing misconduct and JR non-disclosure
key_facts: Joseph Aaron appealed against a Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal decision finding seven allegations proved and imposing two years' suspension, arising from counsel's fees correspondence, 1988 conveyancing sharp practice, failure to pay OSS compensation to Mr O'Callaghan, and alleged non-disclosure on an ex parte judicial review application.
Aaron had prior Tribunal findings in 1994 and 1998; proceedings accumulated over many years with adjournments linked to his abandoned JR application to Silber J during a part-heard hearing.

The Court quashed findings on negligent misleading of the Tribunal about counsel G's fees and on misleading the Administrative Court, but upheld conveyancing, OSS non-compliance and delay in replying to regulatory correspondence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 49 Solicitors Act 1974 to the Administrative Court by way of rehearing against conviction and two-year suspension.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal partially allowed: misleading-Tribunal and judicial-review non-disclosure findings quashed; suspension reduced from two years to one year.
enrichment.ratio: Article 6 reasonable time in solicitor discipline engages only post-institution delay and did not require quashing here; a tribunal need not recuse itself from misconduct arising from its own adjournment where no real possibility of bias exists; negligent but non-deliberate misstatement to a tribunal may fall below misconduct; ex parte JR applicants satisfy full and frank disclosure by properly communicating urgent supporting documents to the court, not by guaranteeing judicial consideration.
legal_issues: Whether cumulative delay violated Article 6 or amounted to abuse of process
Whether the original Tribunal should have recused itself from the judicial review misconduct allegations
Whether negligent misstatement about counsel fees constituted conduct unbefitting
Whether refusal to admit conveyancing expert evidence was erroneous
Whether Aaron failed to make full and frank disclosure to Silber J

enrichment.short_title: Marine reinsurance premium recovery — privity, broker liability and limitation
key_facts: Heath Lambert, Lloyd's placing broker, sought unpaid 1996 facultative marine reinsurance premiums totalling over $500,000 from Venezuelan broker Scort and fronting insurer Banesco relating to INC's dredger ICOA and other vessels.
Extensions were requested by Scort and confirmed by underwriters via scratched slips; no premiums were paid; claim form issued July 2002.

Defendants disputed which party contracted with the broker, whether the broker paid as volunteer, and limitation; the court largely upheld the broker's indemnity case but found most debts time-barred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside permission to serve claim form out of jurisdiction in Venezuela; preliminary issue on reasonable prospect of success under CPR Part 6.
enrichment.outcome: Service set aside except for $261,632.01 premium on the final ICOA extension to 31 December 1996; that claim has reasonable prospects on liability and is not time-barred.
enrichment.ratio: London placing brokers generally assume premium liability to underwriters when placing into the London market; a floating 'subject to Venezuelan law and/or jurisdiction if required' clause leaves English law and section 53 applicable until exercised; 'warranted premium payable on cash basis within 90 days of attachment' grants credit postponing accrual; correspondence reminding that INC had not paid did not acknowledge debt owed by Scort or Banesco to the broker.
legal_issues: Whether Scort or Banesco is privity party liable for premiums to Heath Lambert
Whether Heath Lambert paid underwriters as volunteer without indemnity entitlement
When causes of action accrued and whether 90-day credit applied to extensions
Whether post-limitation letters constituted acknowledgements under section 29(5)

enrichment.short_title: Gate installer injured by buried mains cable — apportionment between owner and contractor

statutes_considered.title: Occupiers Liability Act 1957
provisions: common duty of care to visitors

key_facts: Claimant Terrence Clark was commissioned by touring theatre company Hosier & Dickson (second defendants) to install gates at 25 Short Street, London; building contractor Parr-related works (first defendants) had excavated for gate post bases in 1996.
First defendants or subcontractors unearthed and reburied a mains electric cable without proper protection, recording inaccurate depth and position; they left site after liquidation in October 1996.
On 13 January 1997 Clark drilled into the mislocated unprotected cable and was injured; agreed damages £185,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second defendant's appeal to Court of Appeal against county court equal apportionment of liability between defendants.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; first defendants two-thirds liable, second defendants one-third liable.
enrichment.ratio: Where contractors expose and incompetently rebury a mains cable, provide false location information and fail contractual duties to check services and consult the architect, they bear primary responsibility; an occupier who fails to contact the electricity board after being told of the cable shares lesser blame but does not equate to the contractors' culpability.
legal_issues: Apportionment of liability between building contractor and occupier for injury caused by hidden mains cable
Contractual duties in building contract as to services, supervision and subcontractor responsibility
Occupiers' common duty of care under the 1957 Act

statutes_considered.title: Rules of the Supreme Court Order 106

key_facts: Peter Pybus appealed out of time against a Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal order striking him off for three proved allegations: non-compliant books of account, failure to comply with a 1994 inadequate professional services decision, and failure to comply with a 2000 adjudicator resolution.
This was his third disciplinary appearance after fines in 1993 and 2000; previous appeals had also been filed late and refused.

enrichment.ratio: Written Tribunal findings filed after an announced order under section 48 are authoritative over brief oral remarks; breach of Solicitors' Accounts Rules and persistent failure to comply with regulatory directions constitute serious conduct warranting strike-off where the solicitor shows no acceptance of responsibility; third late appeal does not excuse meritless challenge.

Whether written findings inconsistent with Chairman's oral remarks invalidate the decision
